q: Every week, Ali ____ the report.
e: The present simple expresses a repeated routine; a third-person singular subject takes the -s form.

q: After the committee ____ the proposal, it announced its decision.
e: The past perfect clearly places the review before the later past announcement.

q: I ____ the door and ____ into the room.
e: Successive completed past actions are normally narrated in the past simple.

q: Ali ____ in Karachi for five years, but now lives elsewhere.
e: A finished period that no longer continues takes the past simple.

q: By the time the meeting began, Ali ____ the letter.
e: The past perfect marks an action completed before another past action.

q: At 8 p.m. yesterday, Omar ____ the letter.
e: The past continuous describes an action in progress at a specified past time.

q: Ali ____ the report for two hours before the supervisor arrived.
e: The past perfect continuous emphasises duration before a past reference point.

q: Ali ____ the report yesterday.
e: A finished action at a definite past time takes the past simple.

q: When I called, Ali ____ dinner.
e: The past continuous shows the background action in progress when another past action occurred.

q: Look at those dark clouds; it ____ rain.
e: “Be going to” expresses a prediction based on present evidence.

q: The train ____ at 6:30 tomorrow morning.
e: The present simple is used for fixed timetables and schedules.

q: We ____ the director at noon tomorrow; the appointment is confirmed.
e: The present continuous can express a definite personal arrangement.

q: I will call you as soon as the meeting ____.
e: Future time clauses after “as soon as” normally use the present simple, not “will.”

q: This time tomorrow, Ali ____ the report.
e: The future continuous describes an action in progress at a future time.

q: By Friday, Ali ____ the letter.
e: The future perfect expresses completion before a specified future time.

q: By next month, Ali ____ here for ten years.
e: The future perfect continuous emphasises duration up to a future point.

q: I think Ali ____ the notice tomorrow.
e: “Will” is commonly used for a prediction or opinion about the future.

q: At the clinic, Zara asked, “____ I borrow your pen while I finish the letter?”
e: “May” is a formal modal for asking permission.

q: A notice signed by Amina at the office states: “Visitors ____ enter this area without permission or the required report.”
e: “Must not” expresses prohibition, not absence of necessity.

q: According to the letter kept at the library, Ali ____ swim when five years old.
e: “Could” expresses general ability in the past.

q: After the session at the clinic, Sana advised a colleague, “You ____ see a doctor if the pain continues.”
e: “Should” is used to give advice.

q: When Sana reached the clinic, the lights were off and the article was gone; the staff ____ have left already.
e: “Must have + past participle” expresses a strong logical deduction about the past.

q: Regarding the report at the museum, Sara said, “You ____ have told me earlier; I could have helped.”
e: “Should have + past participle” expresses criticism or regret about a past action.

q: For Iqra's event at the clinic, you ____ bring food with your notice; refreshments will be provided.
e: “Do not have to” means there is no necessity.

q: While working on the report at the garden, Ali asked, “____ you please close the window?”
e: “Would you please…?” is a polite request form.
